citations.citation: John Moses and Joseph Kirkland (eds.), History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (Chicago and New York: Munsell & Co., 1895). Read here for the town before 1836: the immigration chapter 'From Village to City - 1830 to 1837 - the Balloon Age' at printed pages 78-79 and 87-101, the early taverns and hotels at pages 560-561, the 'Real Estate and Insurance' chapter at pages 541-542, the packing trade at page 389, the fire department at pages 207-208, the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy quoted from Blanchard at page 35, and the Biographical sketches of P. F. W. Peck, Philo Carpenter, John Dean Caton and Alexander N. Fullerton at pages 570-577 and 584; and, for the shore of 1812 (T-0471), the chapter 'The Massacre' at pages 49-50, 54 and 60-61 - the low, discontinuous sand-hills south of Twelfth Street, the scattered cottonwoods on the bank's lower reaches, and the two 'Massacre trees' of Eighteenth Street with Mrs. Kinzie's word that they were saplings in 1812.

transcribes.note: PRINTED AT LENGTH AND NOT MERELY CITED. At pages 34-35 the volume introduces the Kinzie and Clybourn genealogy as 'best told by Rufus Blanchard ... He says:' and sets the whole passage as a block quotation, which is why bk_mose1_019 - Benjamin Hall's 1830 arrival and the town's first tannery - is a reading of Blanchard through Moses and Kirkland and not of Moses and Kirkland. This project does not hold Blanchard and cannot check the transcription. Blanchard in turn credits Benjamin Hall himself for the detail, so the chain to the fact is three deep and the claim says so.
transcribes.work: Rufus Blanchard, Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (Wheaton, Ill.: R. Blanchard & Co., 1881)

what_it_does_not_supply: MOST OF WHAT IT WAS FETCHED FOR. Of the forty-nine lead surnames the Newberry index flagged against this work, thirteen earned a claim, twenty-one appear only outside the pre-1836 window, eight appear early and say nothing usable, one (`black`) is only ever the adjective, four are unresolved because the volume carries a surname one character from the index card's spelling, and two are absent outright. The full row-by-row result is committed at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v1_lead_surnames.json so the next run does not pay for the search twice.

VOLUME 2, WHICH IS HALF THE WORK. Only volume 1 is read. The Newberry cards do not say which volume they cite, so an absence recorded here may simply be in the other book, and every ABSENT verdict in the lookup file says so on itself.

AN INDEPENDENT VOICE. It is a compilation of 1895 and it names its own authorities on the pages read: Andreas for Garrett's $1,800,000 of auction sales, Bross's History of Chicago page 38 for the earliest deeds, the Story of Chicago page 130 for Caton's election tally, Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pages 37-8 for the pre-1830 settler list, S. R. Beggs's West and Northwest page 95 for the Black Hawk alarm, and Rufus Blanchard's Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (1881) quoted at length for the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy. Where the sentence itself credits another work, the claim says so and the citation must go to that work and not to this one.
A SINGLE ADDRESS IN THE MODERN SENSE, and no street numbers. Positions here are corners, lots, blocks, a river bank and a tree.

ANY DATE FINER THAN THE YEAR for two things this project wanted finer: Caton's marriage, which is given as '1835' with the scene date sitting in the middle of it, and the Hubbard-Marsh packing partnership, which is 'later'.

CONSISTENCY WITH ITSELF. Page 89 dates Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings to 1832 while page 570 has Peck's occupied in the fall of 1831; page 207 forms the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company on 7 October 1835 while page 570 has it organised on 20 October 1835. Both readings of each are recorded and neither is adopted.
what_it_supplies: A TRADE CENSUS OF THE WHOLE TOWN, at page 95: the State census taken between 1 September and December 1835 counted 3,297 people, forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room. The project had no denominator for its business layer and this is one - for December 1835 and not for July.

A BUILDING WITH FOUR OF THE FIVE FIELDS data/structures/ WANTS, at page 90: John S. C. Hogan's story-and-a-half log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, at the angle where Lake and South Water streets meet, with the post office partitioned off inside it from 2 November 1832.

TWO RESIDENCES STATED AS SUCH, which is the field the town is thinnest in: Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging and keeping his study in the second storey of Peck's store from May 1833 (page 571), and John Dean Caton renting the back room and attic of Dr Temple's Temple Building from December 1833, sleeping in the attic and practising law in the back room, and sub-letting desk-room in it to his competitor Spring (page 577).

BUSINESSES GIVEN BY CORNER, LOT OR LANDMARK: Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings at the south-east corners of South Water and Dearborn and of South Water and La Salle (page 89); Peck's two-storey frame store of black walnut brought from Detroit, occupied in the fall of 1831 (page 570); Sylvester Marsh killing beef under an old elm on the open prairie at what became Monroe Street from the winter of 1833-4 (page 389); William Jones's lots 2 and 7 in block 17 fronting Water and Lake (page 542).

OCCUPATIONS AND ARRIVALS for men this project already holds: Philo Carpenter as the town's first druggist, arriving within a month before 19 August 1832; Benjamin Hall as proprietor of the first tannery ever established there, arriving 1830; Dole, Clybourn, the Noble brothers and Gurdon S. Hubbard beginning the slaughtering and packing trade in 1832; the 1833 spring arrivals including Caton, Kimball and Asahel Pierce; and Hubbard's permanent residence dated to 1832 by the compiler's own reason for leaving him off a list.

TWO PRESENCE LISTS: the twenty-two men who signed the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company roll on 7 October 1835 (pages 207-208), and, unread and left for its own ticket, the 'LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830' at pages 78-79, about thirty rows with nativity, year and remarks columns.
ONE STATEMENT ABOUT THE GROUND OF THE SCENE, at page 79: the winter of 1834-5 was open, with little snow, front doors standing open all winter, and cattle living on grass on the river bank.

citations.carries_no_document: Opened and read in full 2026-08-11 (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chicago_River&action=raw, HTTP 200). Looked for a transcription of Swearingen's 1803 journal and there is none: the page paraphrases him in one sentence of its own prose and footnotes the reprinting, which is a citation and not a reprinting. Every other passage this project draws on here is the same shape. So this record's rung is a judgement about an encyclopedia article — later scholarship, tier 4 — and the documents behind it have to be fetched on their own terms. Where it sends you: Quaife 1913, pp. 373-377 for Swearingen; Holland, Chicago in Maps (2005), pp. 102-109 and Andreas vol. 1, pp. 234-235 for the harbour works.

endings.text: Your note reads: in by the end of the north pier, past the light, up under the Dearborn draw. By autumn that pier will be 1,260 feet into the lake, so your mark will want redrawing. A harbour that keeps growing is a good problem to have.
Your note reads: in between the piers, past the light at the mouth, up under the Dearborn draw to the forwarding houses. Of everything on it, the light is the one mark that stays put this summer.

evidence.locator: 1 July 1835, p. 4, col. 4, the card headed 'NEWBERRY & [DOLE,] Storage, Forwarding and C[ommission] MERCHAN[TS]' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_07_01#c015). Transcription-mediated reading; the brackets are the transcription's.
evidence.text: In the Chicago Democrat of 1 July 1835, Newberry & Dole advertise as storage, forwarding and commission merchants and agents for the Merchants' Line, and also as wholesale and retail dealers in dry goods, groceries and provisions.

evidence.reasoning: The trade style and the Merchants' Line agency are the firm's own words on 1 July 1835; that their goods came by lake is read from the agency and from the 1834 season's 180 arrivals reported in the same paper. No particular consignment is claimed.
evidence.text: A forwarding and commission house received goods landed from lake vessels and sent them on to, or sold them for, other traders; a walk from such a house to the harbour follows that freight back the way it came.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record newberry_dole_warehouse, whose position is reconstructed and whose note carries both readings without settling them. The stop says the bank is disputed and claims no front door.
evidence.text: Where Newberry & Dole's warehouse stood is disputed: one dossier reads the south bank on South Water Street, Andreas puts the firm's warehouse on the north bank east of the later Rush Street bridge. The scene places it on the south bank as a reconstruction, so the stop claims the firm, not the spot.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, the lighthouse paragraph containing 'Before it was fairly completed, however, on October 30, of that year, the structure fell' and 'Another tower, forty feet high, was begun and completed by Mr. Jackson in 1832.'
evidence.text: Andreas: the first lighthouse tower fell on 30 October 1831, before it was fairly completed; another tower, forty feet high, was begun and completed by Mr. Jackson in 1832, and it boasted of a fourteen-inch reflector.

evidence.locator: Lighthousefriends, Chicago Harbor lighthouse page (light ID 234), the history paragraphs on the 1832 tower: 'This lighthouse stood forty feet high and employed four, fourteen-inch reflectors in its bird-cage lantern room.'
evidence.text: Lighthousefriends: the 1832 tower was the first light established on Lake Michigan, forty feet high, with four fourteen-inch reflectors in its bird-cage lantern room.

evidence.reasoning: The structure record grades the function harbour_light attested on both sources; what a harbour light is for is read from the kind of thing it is. The stop claims no keeper, no lighting schedule and no vessel that steered by it.
evidence.text: A light at the river's mouth gave vessels on the lake a mark for the harbour entrance after dark.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record chicago_lighthouse_1832, which reads the coordinate off Wright's sheet through the project's fitted affine and grades it inferred.
evidence.text: The tower is placed on the Fort Dearborn Reservation west of the fort, at the inside of the bend where the river had turned south, from the ring lettered 'L. House' on Wright's 1834 map.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record and docs/RESEARCH/chicago_lighthouse_1832.md, which trace 'conical' and 'masonry' to neither source and leave the shape to a liberty. The stop calls the shape our reconstruction.
evidence.text: Only the tower's height and its lantern are documented. Its taper, cap, finish and diameter as drawn are the scene's reconstruction, and its stone is an inference from the fallen first tower's three-foot walls by the same contractor.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record's function note, which records the gap rather than filling it. The stop names no keeper for the scene date and meets no one.
evidence.text: Samuel Lasby was the first keeper; who kept the light on 1 July 1835 was not established by any source reached.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, the bridges section, Norton's letter beginning 'I came to Chicago November 16, 1833' and Andreas's correction 'Mr. Norton is evidently in error as to the time of the completion of the bridge'; with 'The first drawbridge thrown across the river was at Dearborn Street'. Read in the chicagology Dearborn Street bridges transcription.
evidence.text: Nelson R. Norton, a ship-carpenter, writes in a letter Andreas prints that he cut the lumber for a drawbridge over the winter of 1833-34 and began building it in March 1834; Andreas notes the Democrat has it formally accepted by the Trustees in August. It was the first drawbridge across the river.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, scan p. 415 (per docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 4), the paragraph on the Dearborn Street drawbridge, read verbatim in the chicagology Dearborn Street bridges transcription.
evidence.text: Andreas: 'From various sources it is learned that it was about three hundred feet long, and the opening for the passage of craft about sixty feet.' It was of the 'gallows pattern', with frames one at either end of the draw.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record's change note, which reads the repairs from Andreas and says no source dates or describes them closely enough to model; the stop says only that it was struck and patched more than once.
evidence.text: The bridge was paid for repairs in September 1834 and repaired again in 1835 and 1837; vessels passing the draw struck it.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record dearborn_street_drawbridge, which places the crossing on the street it is named for and grades the position inferred. The jaunt stops at the south end and does not cross.
evidence.text: The bridge crosses the main stem in line with Dearborn Street, its south abutment at the foot of Dearborn on South Water Street.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, the harbour section (scan pp. 487 and 489 per docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 3), 'the north (weather) pier'; Wikipedia, Chicago River, the harbour improvement paragraphs.
evidence.text: The north pier is the weather pier of the federal harbour works, the northern of two piers holding open the 1834 cut through the sand bar at the river's mouth.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, the harbour section (scan pp. 261 and 487 per docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 3), on the work begun under Major Bender in 1833.
evidence.text: The south pier is the southern of the two piers holding open the 1834 cut; Andreas has the harbour work begun on the south side of the river in June 1833 under Major George Bender, commandant of Fort Dearborn.

evidence.locator: 21 Jan 1835, p. 3, col. 2, 'Chicago Harbor, Illinois.—The operations of constructing an artificial harbor at this place' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_01_21#c001). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: The Democrat printed from the federal Public Documents that one hundred and eighty vessels arrived and discharged their cargoes at Chicago between the opening of navigation and 30 November 1834, and that the harbour should be perfected as rapidly as circumstances permit.

evidence.locator: 25 Mar 1835, p. 3, col. 3, 'Chicago Harbor.—We learn from a friend at Washington' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_03_25#c002). Transcription-mediated reading; the paper reports it second-hand and says so.
evidence.text: The Democrat learns from a friend at Washington that $32,800 has been appropriated by Congress towards the completion of the harbour.

evidence.locator: p. 91, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12304-12307 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: In 1834 'the schooner Illinois, the first large vessel to enter the river, sailed into the harbor amid the rejoicings of the people'.

evidence.locator: p. 95, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12811-12817 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: The first drawbridge, at Dearborn Street, built in 1834 with Nelson R. Norton as contractor, 'was 300 feet in length, by sixteen in width, and had a double draw'.

evidence.locator: p. 91, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12275-12286 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: The first lighthouse tower, fifty feet high, fell before it was completed; another, forty feet high, was put up in 1832 with a fourteen-inch reflector. 'Samuel S. Lasby was the first, and Mark Beaubien the last keeper of the old light house.'

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, scan p. 503, the opening of the harbour.
evidence.text: On 12 July 1834 the schooner Illinois, the first vessel through the new harbour cut, was cheered at Newberry & Dole’s wharf.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure records north_pier and south_pier, whose lengths are interpolated between year-end figures (Andreas vol. 1, scan pp. 487 and 489 per docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 3, and Wikipedia's harbour summary) and graded inferred. The stop calls the lengths our estimate and says both piers were growing.
evidence.text: No source gives either pier's length on 1 July 1835. The north pier was about 700 feet at the end of 1834 and had been extended to 1,260 feet into the lake by the end of the 1835 season; Andreas has the south pier extended 500 feet in 1835, to 700 in all. The scene draws interpolations, about 900 and 400 feet.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the position notes of the structure records south_pier and north_pier, which measure both lines through the project's fitted affine and grade them inferred. Neither deck has a modelled approach, so the stop is a look from the shore and claims no walk along either pier.
evidence.text: Both piers' lines are read off Wright's 1834 map, the two red lines with HARBOR lettered between them; the south pier's root is on the reservation shore at the river's mouth, and the north pier stands across the channel from it.

The walk, its order, the route note and its two marks, the endings, the timing inputs and the Knows the Harbor keepsake are invented connective narrative. No vessel, cargo, keeper, bridge-tender or customer is documented here, and no named person is met.

opening.text:
JAUNT: ALONG THE WORKING HARBOR. A summer morning, and the lake is the town's highway. Three years ago Chicago had no harbour at all, only a river choked by a sand bar. Then the army cut through the bar, the piers went out into the lake, and in 1834 'the schooner Illinois, the first large vessel to enter the river, sailed into the harbor amid the rejoicings of the people'. That year 180 vessels unloaded here.

Follow the freight back the way it came: from a forwarding house on the river, under the Dearborn Street draw and past the lighthouse, out to the piers, both still pushing into the lake.

premise: Follow freight back to the lake: a forwarding house on the river, the Dearborn Street draw, the light at the mouth, and the two piers still being pushed into the lake. Leave with a route note.

stops.narrative: What the town cannot make, the lake brings.
stops.text: Start at Newberry & Dole's warehouse on the river. In the Democrat of 1 July 1835 they advertise storage, forwarding and commission, agents for the Merchants' Line: goods off the lake land at houses like theirs and go on to every store in town. When the schooner Illinois came up the new channel in July 1834, she was cheered at Newberry & Dole's wharf. Which bank the warehouse stood on is still argued; the trade is not.

stops.narrative: Where the river is crossed, and passed.
stops.text: East to Dearborn Street and the town's first drawbridge, built in 1834 by the ship-carpenter Nelson R. Norton. Moses and Kirkland make it '300 feet in length, by sixteen in width', with 'a double draw'; Andreas gives a sixty-foot opening for craft and gallows frames at either end. Vessels kept striking it, and it was patched in 1834 and again this year. Stay on the south bank.

stops.narrative: A mark for vessels making the river.
stops.text: On along the south bank to the light at the river's mouth, the first on Lake Michigan. The first tower fell in 1831 before it was finished; Mr. Jackson put up this one, forty feet high, in 1832, with a fourteen-inch reflector in the lantern on top. Moses and Kirkland add a surprise: 'Samuel S. Lasby was the first, and Mark Beaubien the last keeper of the old light house.' The town's fiddler and tavern-keeper kept the lighthouse too.

choices.consequence: The light goes on your note: it will stand where you saw it.
choices.label: Mark the light

choices.consequence: The north pier's end goes on your note: it will be further out by autumn.
choices.label: Mark the end of the north pier

stops.narrative: Where the harbour meets the lake.
stops.text: Out to the south pier's root. Across the cut stands the north pier, the weather pier that keeps the sand out. The Democrat printed the federal report: 180 vessels arrived and discharged here in 1834, and Congress has voted $32,800 more toward the harbour. Both piers grow all summer; by the season's end the north pier will reach 1,260 feet into the lake. Choose the mark for your route note.
